chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yusuf ibn Aqeel, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) judged regarding a man who ate, and his companion had a sheep. So he said, 'If you eat it, it is for you, and if you do not eat it, then upon you is such and such (a penalty).' He judged regarding it that this is invalid. There is no fixed amount in eating (sharing food) from the food, whether little of it or much, and he prevented the fine from him.
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on financial liability when sharing food (mu'akalah)?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that Amir al-Mu'minin Ali ibn Abi Talib’s ruling invalidated a claim for a fixed penalty based on the consumption of a shared sheep, establishing that 'mu'akalah' (commensality) does not inherently create a financial debt for the food eaten. This hadith is significant in Shia jurisprudence for distinguishing between social customs of sharing meals and formal contractual obligations, emphasizing that mere consumption does not trigger a specific fine unless explicitly agreed upon. It underscores the principle that customary practices do not automatically generate legal liabilities without clear stipulation.
